newsitem.title: USA: Germany to reopen talks on Jewish reparations.
newsitem.headline: Germany to reopen talks on Jewish reparations.

text.p: The German government has agreed to resume negotiations with Jewish groups on broadening reparation payments for Holocaust victims, including those from former Soviet bloc countries, the World Jewish Congress said on Wednesday.

The move comes after months of criticism of the German government for restricting payments to Holocaust survivors while extending pension benefits to thousands of former members of Hitler's SS around the world.

A WJC spokesman said the negotiations would start in mid-August in Bonn. At issue are restrictions placed on a fund set up by the Germans in 1993 to aid survivors who had not previously received help.

Since the early 1950s, the German government has paid about $50 billion in reparations to Holocaust survivors. The fund was created after the reunification of Germany and was designed to make up for the refusal of the former East Germany to pay reparations to Hitler's victims.
Under the fund's provisions, 27,000 survivors are receiving about $300 a month.
But the WJC, whose secretary general, Israel Singer, is the head of the committee negotiating with the Germans, said tens of thousands of others did not qualify because of the fund's restrictions.

The WJC wants to liberalise the criteria to include Holocaust victims still in former Soviet bloc countries, people forced into military and labour camps, people forced into hiding under false identification papers and applicants who earn more than $16,000 a year.
Under current fund guidelines, a victim must have spent a mininimum of six months in a concentration camp or 18 months in a forced ghetto.

Elan Steinberg, the WJC executive director, praised the German decision to resume negotiations, saying,"Germany has undertaken an extraordinary effort in its reparations payments. It would have been tragic if in the last phase of this process, all the goodwill that has been built up over the years was lost over relatively small sums."
Negotiations will be conducted by the Conference on Jewish Material Claims against Germany and the German Federal Republic.
